title: The Programme Post
strapline: An evidence-led view of delivery, decisions and the people moving work forward.
intro: A newspaper should make the important things easy to find, and the evidence easy to follow. This fictional edition shows the format using five different source types.

articles.title: Rehearsal complete; release decision awaits two checks
articles.dek: The fictional Meridian programme has finished its rehearsal. Rollback evidence and an access review still stand between progress and a release decision.
articles.label: Illustrative story

paragraphs.text: The operational rehearsal is complete and six runbooks have been reviewed, according to the demonstration update. The same update explicitly separates rehearsal results from release authorization.

The programme lead’s fictional decision note says approval has not been granted. It identifies rollback evidence and the access review as the two remaining checks, with evidence to be considered on 10 November.
The delivery snapshot records 84 completed checks out of 100. That is a completion measure for the listed workstreams, not a release-readiness score or a statement that all controls have passed.

articles.title: One shared denominator brings the picture into focus
articles.dek: The demo workbook and chat agree on 84 completed checks. The remaining 16 are not automatically 16 blockers.
articles.label: Illustrative story

paragraphs.text: A clarification in the fictional Teams thread identifies 100 as the scope of the current snapshot, not the number completed. The workbook reconciles to 84 completed checks across five workstreams.
Client onboarding shows 14 of 20 checks complete, while data controls shows 16 of 20. The workbook labels both “Watch”; it does not provide evidence for a change in delivery date.

articles.title: A proposed window is not an approved date
articles.dek: The transcript preserves an important distinction between a planning discussion and a commitment.
articles.label: Illustrative story

paragraphs.text: In the synthetic readiness review, the facilitator describes the week of 16 November as a possible release window. The speaker explicitly calls it a proposal.
The decision note says no production release date has been committed. The next review is due on 10 November, after the remaining evidence is considered.

articles.title: Two owners, one clear evidence deadline
articles.dek: The demonstration transcript records specific follow-ups without inventing new commitments.
articles.label: Illustrative story

paragraphs.text: The operations lead takes responsibility for the rollback walkthrough by 9 November. The control owner separately undertakes to finish the access-review evidence pack by the same date.
These are role labels from a fictional transcript, not identified employees. The actions shown below retain their stated owners and dates.

articles.title: Six runbooks give the handover a common reference
articles.dek: A small operational detail can carry more value than a broad statement of confidence.
articles.label: Illustrative story

paragraphs.text: The demo update reports six reviewed runbooks and a shared index for the delivery team. It says each runbook has a role owner in the fictional scenario.
Reviewing the runbooks is one recorded preparation step. The decision email still requires the two outstanding checks before a release decision.

actions.text: Complete the rollback walkthrough and bring the evidence.
Review both checks before making a release decision.

limitations: All stories, numbers, dates, names of programmes and role labels are fictional. No email, Teams conversation or bank system was accessed to create this demonstration.
No public news was imported. A real edition should read and cite freely accessible first-party sources rather than invent a current headline.
The HTML is an offline snapshot. Source popovers explain attribution; they do not grant access to private originals or refresh the reporting.
